blocks.text: Philippe Jarrigeon: Reality in a state of disquiet.

What if nature were, ultimately, the most sophisticated set of all? The question may seem paradoxical when it comes to Philippe Jarrigeon , a photographer whose images have long embraced artifice, staging, vivid colours and unlikely juxtapositions. With him, nothing is entirely left to chance. An object becomes a character, a body becomes a sculpture, a flower can take on the appearance of a creature, and the ordinary, carefully displaced, slips into the strange. His photographs possess the precision of commissioned imagery, coupled with the irony of a slightly deranged world.

With Le Vrai du Faux , presented at Paris Photo 2026 in the Émergence section and awarded the Maison Ruinart Prize, Philippe Jarrigeon does not abandon this logic of construction: he simply shifts its setting. Following Rocher Fatal , created in the Forest of Fontainebleau, he now turns his gaze towards the Faux de Verzy, those twisted beech trees of Champagne whose silhouettes seem to have emerged from a fantastical fiction. Around them appear shells, bouquets, luminous forms and ambiguous objects. A vanished sea resurfaces in a shell; centuries of history can be read in a branch; the living world sometimes seems to have been sculpted by an invisible hand.

What is striking, then, is not so much the transition from artifice to nature as their strange convergence. Philippe Jarrigeon discovers in the natural world what he had already been creating in his images: forms that resist immediate recognition. Nature itself becomes scenographer, sculptor, almost a plastic artist. It produces its own monsters, its own sets, its own illusions.

Le Vrai du Faux therefore plays less on the opposition between reality and fiction than on their mutual contamination. What is a photograph when what we are looking at seems to have been staged, even though no one staged it? At what point does a tree become a character? When does a shell cease to be a simple object and become the trace of a vanished world? And above all: how much fiction do we ourselves introduce into what we believe we are seeing?

Perhaps this is where Philippe Jarrigeon’s work is shifting today. He no longer necessarily constructs the uncanny: he finds it. His photographic gesture is therefore less about fabricating a world than revealing the one that already exists — framing it, displacing it, making it subtly waver.

From then on, the real and the false are no longer two opposing categories. They become two sides of the same image. And between them, Philippe Jarrigeon creates the territory he has always been drawn to: the place where reality suddenly begins to look like fiction.

Current News : Philippe Jarrigeon presents Rocher Fatal , his second book, devoted to the Forest of Fontainebleau, while his solo exhibition is on view at Womanray until December 24. @womanraygallery
He is also the winner of the 2026 Maison Ruinart Prize for Le Vrai du Faux , a new project created in Champagne around the Faux de Verzy, trees, seashells and geological memory. @ruinart

Your first photographic trigger? Philippe Jarrigeon: I think my first real epiphany came when I discovered Natacha Lesueur’s work, particularly her photographs of teeth made from beans… That was when I became particularly interested in fine-art photography. It was an image published in Mouvement magazine. I was a student, and it made me laugh. She later became my teacher at ECAL, and we eventually became friends.

A photographic memory from your childhood? P.J.: I remember my parents’ photo booths. I was always rather surprised to see them changing hairstyles from one photograph to the next. It’s quite a funny memory.

The camera of your childhood? P.J.: I still have the camera I used back in middle school: a Canon EOS 300. I love it. It’s unpretentious, sturdy, not particularly fragile, and takes beautiful photographs. I mainly take it on holiday and, in the end, those are often the images I still like best.

The one you use today? P.J.: Today I use different camera bodies, notably a Mamiya IQ150 and a Fujifilm GFX, and sometimes a Polaroid. I really enjoy moving from one technique to another, from digital to analogue. I find that this alternation keeps the eye in motion, cultivating a certain flexibility, almost an elasticity of the optic nerve. It’s also a way of avoiding being trapped in a single way of photographing.

The man or woman in an image who inspired you? P.J.: I think it’s David Hockney. I discovered his work quite early, almost unconsciously, through an exhibition poster my parents had hung in our living room. They actually spent a good part of their lives trying to make their home look like one of his paintings! So that image accompanied me from childhood. Later, as I became more interested in his work, but also in his life and personality, I discovered the man behind the images. I think he deeply influenced me, although I only realised it much later.
The image you wish you had made? P.J.: Bigger, Splash by David Hockney.
The one that moved you the most? P.J.: I’m thinking of Pastel Cats (2000), a photograph by Tim Walker that particularly moved me.
And the one that made you angry? P.J.: I’m a very calm person.
Which photograph changed the world? P.J.: Neil Armstrong’s first steps on the moon, photographed by Buzz Aldrin on July 20, 1969. If all of that is true…
A key image in your personal pantheon? P.J.: Without hesitation, one of Man Ray’s portraits of William Wegman’s famous dog. I could choose any one of them.
What interests you most in an image? P.J.: The photographer’s intention, and then the inaccuracies, the out-of-frame elements…
What details do you look for in a face, a landscape or an object? P.J.: I’m interested in all forms of enchantment. Amusement parks, charming objects and smiling faces.

Elliott Erwitt said: “Colour is descriptive. Black and white is interpretative.” Do you agree? P.J.: I would rather say that black and white gives images a ghostly quality, a kind of timelessness. Colour, on the other hand, is more of a seduction tool. It attracts and captures the eye, creating an immediate emotion.

In your opinion, can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? P.J.: Emotion first, without hesitation. Technique is a means, never an end in itself. An image can be technically perfect and yet provoke nothing.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic? P.J.: It all depends on what we mean by aesthetic. I don’t believe beauty is something superficial; quite the opposite. It is a subject in its own right, a way of looking at the world and presenting oneself to it. I actually believe it can be found everywhere.
What elements can make silence visible in a photograph? P.J.: Photography, for me, is the art of the out-of-frame, the art of suggestion.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from the staging? P.J.: I’m more drawn to staging, but what interests me precisely is leaving room for the unexpected, managing to capture it within a device that has been thought out and constructed beforehand. A photograph becomes unique when it manages to make something unexpected emerge from a moment that has nevertheless been entirely orchestrated. It is this tension between control and accident that interests me.
Can a photograph be truer than reality? P.J.: An image, even when staged, even when it is the product of imagination, always begins with reality. The imaginary is far more real than it appears.

Can a photograph change our perception of an event? P.J.: Absolutely. For that, all you have to do is look at birthday photographs: you never really know whether people are happy or devastated about getting older… And yet that is what remains of this kind of event: a forced smile.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? P.J.: Photography is the testimony of a form of manipulation. Every image is a construction, a point of view, a choice. It frames, excludes and transforms reality. In that sense, it always contains a part of falsehood, and that is precisely what interests me: its ability to manufacture another truth.

What makes a good photograph? P.J.: I believe everything starts with intention. It is neither colour, nor format, nor framing or light that, on their own, make a good photograph. These are parameters, sometimes almost technical prerequisites. What matters is the attention brought to the starting point, followed by the photographer’s ability to allow themselves to be surprised by what they themselves have initiated. And sometimes that surprise only reveals itself afterwards, when looking at a contact sheet. So I would say that a good photograph is, above all, one that can still surprise us — including its own author.

In your opinion, what quality is necessary to be a good photographer? P.J.: Curiosity, combined with a good dose of audacity and perseverance. It is what pushes you to observe, to explore, to take an interest in other people and in the world, and above all never to consider your way of seeing as something acquired.

How do you choose your projects? P.J.: Above all, with the heart, as much as possible. There has to be a sense of evidence, a desire… Then you also have to remain pragmatic: you don’t always get to choose everything, and some subjects eventually choose us too. In the end, it’s a balance between desire and reality.

How would you describe your creative process? P.J.: Before embarking on a photographic adventure, I always go through a long research phase. First I identify a subject, a territory, an idea, and then I immerse myself completely in it: I consult archives, explore its lexical, visual and cultural field, and try to understand all its resonances. This phase can take a long time. Then I let things settle. The first intuitions emerge, I start making sketches, sometimes very rough ones, writing down ideas, desires and possible staging approaches. Then comes the time to make the work. Ultimately, my process is not so far removed from that of a film director: there is a phase of scouting, introspection, writing, and then implementation. Photography is almost the culmination of all that preparatory work.

A recent project that is particularly close to your heart? P.J.: I took part in Paris Photo, where I presented three exhibitions, while also accompanying the release of my second book, Rocher Fatal , devoted to the Forest of Fontainebleau. It’s quite an intense period, with several projects taking shape simultaneously. The next step will be editing the film I made alongside the production of the Rocher Fatal images. And then I’ll begin work on my third book, which will probably take me towards Egypt. It’s a new territory I’m very keen to explore.
The person you would like to photograph? P.J.: Isabelle Huppert!
The person you would like to be photographed by? P.J.: Cindy Sherman!
An essential photography book? P.J.: Le manuel de la photo ratée by Thomas Lélu.
What was the last photograph you took? P.J.: A photograph of the people assembling the stands at Paris Photo. 🙂
On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook or TikTok — and why? P.J.: Instagram, although there’s no reason apart from my age, perhaps.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media? P.J.: Absolutely everything has changed. Social media has profoundly altered our relationship with images, their circulation, production and reception. Photography has become a permanent stream, almost an element of everyday life, which forces us to invent new ways of looking, of taking time, and of preserving a more singular relationship with images. There is nevertheless something very positive about this evolution: photography has become more inclusive, more accessible and more participatory. More perspectives have emerged, boundaries have shifted, and this makes the photographic landscape much more vibrant and, in a way, more fun. But yes, fundamentally, everything has changed.

An Instagram account to follow without fail? P.J.: I would say Aline Rüede, behind the account @studiovegete. She is a floral designer who notably accompanied and helped me a great deal in creating the flower portraits for my latest project, Rocher Fatal . I particularly like her universe and sensitivity, which I invite you to discover.

What is your view on AI? P.J.: I find AI interesting, particularly because of the dialogue it makes possible between humans and machines. It’s a tool that allows us to move forward, step back, test, shift our ideas and explore territories we might not have thought of on our own. In that respect, I find the exchange stimulating and invigorating. My real reservation lies elsewhere: in the concentration of power that it entails. I’m somewhat wary of the fact that the tools now shaping our relationship with images, information and, more broadly, knowledge are in the hands of an extremely small number of players. As long as there is a genuine balance between human intelligence and the machine, everything is fine; otherwise… it’s George Orwell. I keep a few shamanic contacts safely tucked away… just in case.
Colour or black and white? P.J.: Colour.
Natural light or artificial light? P.J.: Artificial.
Which city seems the most photogenic to you? P.J.: Disneyland!
The city, country or culture you dream of discovering? P.J.: I’d like to spend more time in Cairo, Egypt.
The place you never tire of? P.J.: The Forest of Fontainebleau!
The image that, for you, represents the current state of the world? P.J.: The fires that devastated the Forest of Fontainebleau last summer.
In your opinion, what is missing from the world today? P.J.: A better distribution of wealth.
If God existed, would you ask him to pose for you, or would you opt for a selfie with him? P.J.: A selfie with God, without hesitation. Classy.
Your favourite drug? P.J.: Success, business, love, chocolate and acid!
Your best way of disconnecting? P.J.: But why disconnect?
Your latest extravagance? P.J.: A Lemaire shirt, so that I could properly receive the Ruinart Prize.
Your greatest professional extravagance? P.J.: Bringing together seven greyhounds and Snoop Dogg in a Scarface -style set.
The profession you would never have wanted to do? P.J.: Guard at the Queen’s Guard in England. Too boring.
Which question throws you off balance the most? P.J.: “So, how are you?”
The last thing you did for the first time? P.J.: Golf. And it really hurts your back!
Your greatest regret? P.J.: Not having been able to photograph David Hockney — it almost happened for Interview magazine.

If you had to start all over again? P.J.: Oh no, please, let’s not start. We continue, and then we stop. As my grandmother used to say in her Creuse dialect, “A life goes by quickly, but you fall in love all your life.” She’s almost a hundred.
If you could organise your ideal dinner, who would be at the table? P.J.: Morticia Addams & Jean Jaurès.

What would you like people to say about you… afterwards? P.J.: I’d rather they told me things beforehand or while I’m alive! I think exchange is always more interesting and constructive when it happens while someone is still alive. I’m not much of a fan of posthumous conversations!
The one thing people absolutely need to know about you? P.J.: I’m funny. Really.
One last word? P.J.: Thank you.
